entities.label: TextOfTheConstitution
entities.rationale: The text of the Constitution is a specific information artifact whose content (the pattern of linguistic meaning) can be copied, instantiated in multiple physical bearers (parchment, printed copies, digital files), and persists independently of any single material substrate. This makes it a generically dependent continuant (BFO_0000031). It is an individual (a specific document's text content, not a general kind), and it is most proximately an instance of the existing working class Statute (itself typed as BFO_0000031). The existing individual USConstitution is already in the ontology; TextOfTheConstitution is the informational content (the text) rather than the document artifact as a whole, though the distinction may prompt a clarifying question.

relations.rationale: The text of the Constitution is an instance of the Statute class, which is already typed as BFO_0000031 (generically dependent continuant), capturing its character as a normative information artifact.

The text is a part of (or concretely coincides with) the USConstitution individual already in the ontology. Modeling it as a part-of relation captures that the textual content is a component of the broader constitutional document individual.

open_questions: Should 'TextOfTheConstitution' be distinguished from the existing individual 'USConstitution'? If USConstitution is already intended to denote the textual/informational content, we may be able to reuse that individual rather than minting a new one.

Do you want to model 'the text of the Constitution' as strictly the linguistic/information content (BFO_0000031, generically dependent continuant) vs. a physical inscription on parchment (BFO_0000040, material entity)? The BFO distinction matters: the text-as-content is GDC; the parchment document is a material entity.
Should we also assert that TextOfTheConstitution is a bearer of specific LegalExistenceCondition or LegalLegitimacyCondition instances already in the ontology?
proposal.rationale_summary: The text of the Constitution is paradigmatically a generically dependent continuant (BFO_0000031) because its identity is constituted by an information pattern that can be multiply instantiated across physical bearers (manuscripts, printed copies, digital files) without loss of identity. It is not the parchment (a material entity, BFO_0000040) nor a spatial region; it is the informational content. I type it as an individual (a specific text, not a kind of text) and classify it under the existing working class Statute (BFO_0000031). I also assert a BFO part-of relation to the existing USConstitution individual, since that individual likely already denotes the same or encompassing artifact; however, this overlap prompts an open question about whether a new individual is truly needed or whether USConstitution already serves this role.
